title: Long ants standing still in a crowd -- moving, this time
question: Watch both. Does the crowd keep rearranging itself, or is there a clump that sits in one place for the whole loop -- and does what movement there is read as ants sorting themselves out rather than teleporting?
context_md:
Your report, 2026-09-11: *"long ants getting stuck. Not all of them but it happens regularly. It seems like they get stuck in a big group/pile of long ants."*

Same bed, same seed, same 3,000 frames (28,000-31,000), the nest band. **This is the pair you already judged as strips** -- you said you saw a clear stuck clump on one side and nothing so obvious on the other, and you were right: the side with the visible clump is the *changed* one. Here it is as movement instead of stills, which is the reading that matters.

**What changed, and what it does not reach.** A carrying long ant that has nowhere to go waits for the nestmate in its way to move rather than turning round -- and it used to wait for ever, because that nestmate is usually stuck for the same reason. One arm still waits for ever; the other gives it four beats and then turns round.

**The clump you can still see is not long ants.** Censused over three seeds and 120,000 frames, 89% of the animals wedged in a pile have bodies of one or two cells rather than seven, and for those turning round is not a move -- there is nothing to turn. Clumps counting long bodies alone never exceed four animals on any seed, in either arm. Why a long ant ends up one cell long is the next question and nothing here answers it.
